prerequisites: Basic knowledge in the application of balance equations for technical systems

learning_outcomes.text: Participants can describe, analyze, and independently design and optimize (micro)electronic systems, particularly with regard to sustainable, energy-efficient design.
Identify the relevant components for intelligent energy-autonomous systems and relate them to the desired functions of a product.
Understand the connection between energy supply, scalability, flexibility, monetary and ecological costs using application examples.
Quantify the energy consumption of (micro)electronic systems and subsequently know and apply optimization strategies.
Quantitatively describe, design, and calculate energy yields of relevant energy supply technologies and systems.

Critically reflect on the possibilities and limitations of alternative sustainable energy conversion technologies from techno-economic aspects and purposefully plan and deploy energy-autonomous systems.
Carry out the predictive estimation and subsequent calculation of the CO2 'footprint' of realized prototypes, as well as the assessment of further parameters of life cycle assessments.
To later design and optimize such products, components, and systems in all relevant industrial sectors, e.g., in the areas of condition monitoring, industrial digitalization, IoT, etc.

syllabus_topics: Relevance of energy supply for scalable cyber-physical systems, "Edge Computing" and wireless sensor/actuator technology, cost aspects
Definition of "Energy Harvesting" and distinction from renewable energy technology
System structure and properties of intelligent, autonomous microsystems
Quantification and modeling of energy consumption of microsystems, strategy of "Duty-Cycling" and relevance of ultra-energy-efficient sleep states
Properties and simple lifetime calculation of primary storage/batteries
Properties of sustainable energy converters, overview of possible physical conversion principles

Description, design and optimization of the most relevant "Energy-Harvesting-Technologies and Systems, such as photovoltaic, thermal and kinetic converters. Systematic description and calculation based on the following categories:
Description and quantification of the energy supply
Description and quantification of the physical conversion mechanism: properties and ultimate physical limits, loss mechanisms, conversion efficiency, optimization potentials
System design, dealing with intermittent sources and difficult-to-predict energy supply
Practical/product examples, relevance of a value- and not technology-driven development of energy-autonomous systems
Students work on a small team project throughout the semester which includes a certain energy autonomy
Is processed with a view to ecological sustainability
Has the character of a system
Elements such as microprocessors, energy harvesters, power-saving communication via radio, small sensors and actuators can be used.
Due to the variability of the topics addressed, very individual solutions are developed and refined week by week.
Power and material-saving radio-networked door signs, portable power generators for rivers or dynamo-based speedometers for bicycles are some examples of such topics.

assessment_methods.method: Written elaboration and presentation for Laboratory Sustainable Energy-Autonomous Systems (unmarked)

assessment_rules: The module grade for MECB610A corresponds to the grade of MECB611A. MECB611A is assessed as either a 90-minute written exam, three 30-minute intermediate exams during the semester, or a 20-minute oral exam. MECB612A Laboratory Sustainable Energy-Autonomous Systems is ungraded and requires a written elaboration and a 10-minute presentation.
